How Impeller fills in missing expression, one idea at a time

Impeller imputes a spot’s missing genes from two graphs, one of nearby spots and one of spots with similar expression, and reaches far along them with random-walk paths instead of stacking layers. Click any spot of the section to select it, then switch views. Each control changes the tissue right away.

Selected: an L4 spot

Two kinds of neighbours

6 spatial neighbours: the spots right next to it.
8 most similar spots by expression: 8 of 8 in the same layer, the farthest 10.5 spot widths away.

Neighbours on the spatial graph are close by. Similar spots can sit far away along the same layer, because cells of one type share an expression profile.

What stacked GNN layers do

08162432

The selected spot averages over
1
spot, from 1 tissue layer

Each layer replaces every spot’s value with the mean over itself and its spatial neighbours. More layers reach farther, and the thin L4 band washes out: this is over-smoothing.

Paths instead of whole neighbourhoods

Spatial paths reach up to 7 steps away, through 8 spots each.
Similarity paths jump up to 15.5 spot widths in one step.

Impeller samples 8 random walks of length 8 per graph (3 drawn here) and weighs every position with a learned path operator, so one layer reaches 7 steps away without averaging every spot in between.

Paper Lowest error on all 14 datasets and all three metrics; against the best expression-only method, eKNN, the RMSE falls by 11%, 31% and 6% (Table 2). Standard GNNs get worse as their receptive field grows; Impeller has the lowest error at every size and its best at 32 steps (RMSE 0.277, Table 3). Adding either graph to a model built on the other lowers the RMSE in 22 of 24 cases across 12 DLPFC sections (Fig. 2).

Toy data from the Impeller walkthrough: a seeded section of 539 spots in cortical layers L1–L6 and white matter, a 6-nearest-spot spatial graph and an 8-nearest gene similarity graph; the layer marker is G25. Method: Duan et al., Bioinformatics 2024.
